sentences.text: Last time, taking turns took 54 rounds.
And we ended on a promise: let the sliders and the dial step together, and it takes five.
But stepping together is harder than it sounds.
When Dune's slider moved, two episodes ago, the dial's meter moved too.
To step together, every control has to know how its move disturbs every meter.
For five clinics, that is a small table. For 7,000 providers, it is 50 million numbers.
So how can this possibly be fast?
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: the arrow matrix.
Here is that table for our five clinics, at the fit. One row for each meter, one column for each control.
Each cell says how much that meter moves when that control does.
Down the diagonal is each clinic's own wobble, from last time: 6.38 for Alder, 6.66 for Birch, down to 0.02 for Elm.
In the corner is the dial's own: 10.2.
Along the two edges is how strongly each clinic is tied to the dial.
Birch, with 24 higher-risk patients, most of all: 5.94. Elm, with none: zero.
And everywhere else, nothing. Alder's slider cannot move Birch's meter, because no patient belongs to both.
That is not an approximation. It is the model.
Look at the shape it leaves: an arrowhead.
With five clinics, the shape hardly matters. So scale up.
Our crowd of 200 providers, with two risk factors, has a table of 40,804 cells. Only 1,004 of them are not zero.
A national measure, with 7,000 providers and 50 risk factors, has almost 50 million cells. Nearly all of them are empty.
Treat that as an ordinary table, and you are stuck. Use the arrow, and it is easy.
Here is how. Take one clinic at a time.
Square its tie to the dial, divide by its own wobble, and take that away from the corner.
Alder takes away 0.15. Birch, 5.30. Cedar, 1.45. Dune, 0.38. Elm, nothing.
The corner falls from 10.2 to 2.93.
And now the sliders are out of the problem. What is left is one small number, for the dial alone.
That number has a meaning. It adds up, clinic by clinic, how much patients differ in risk from others in their own clinic.
Elm, where every patient is lower-risk, adds nothing. It is Episode 4's idea again: the risk rule is learned inside clinics.
It is also a warning. Ignore the clinics, and the data would seem to say three and a half times as much about the dial as they really do.
So the dial's step takes one division. From the plain guess, it is 1.81.
Then each clinic takes its own step, corrected for what the dial just did.
Watch the machine. One joint step, and the dial reads 1.81. A second: 2.00. A third: 2.0164, the top.
Five steps until the dial stops moving, where taking turns needed 54.
And the trouble with where we put zero? Record the risk factor five units higher, or fifty. The joint path does not change at all.
Each step is three cheap jobs: add up over the patients, fold once for each provider, and solve one small system.
We tried it on 2,000 providers and about 200,000 patients. The fit took well under a second.
Written out as an ordinary table, with a column for every provider, the same data would fill 3.3 gigabytes before any fitting began.
So a separate number for every provider is not a computing problem. It only looked like one.
One caution. The arrow needs every patient to belong to exactly one provider. A second grouping that cuts across the first would break it.
Let's gather it up.
Clinics disturb each other only through the dial, so the table is an arrow.
Fold each clinic into the corner, and one small system is left.
Nothing is approximated. It is last episode's step, taken for everything at once.
And keep an eye on that folded number, 2.93. It says how firmly the data hold the dial in place.
Next time: how sure are we?
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
